mainTopic: Old trees as principal; who is believed in disputes over mortgaged land, sharecropping shares, and field improvements
overview: The amud opens by finishing the answers to a challenge about old trees a married woman inherits. Either the trees aged while she owned them, or they stood in someone else's field, so they were her whole principal. Next comes a mortgage שטר that says 'years' with no number. The מלוה already ate the disputed third year's fruit. רב יהודה says land stays with its owner, and רב כהנא says fruit stays with whoever ate it. The הלכה follows רב כהנא, because the truth can still come out and the court should not have to rule twice. In a case where the מלוה claims five years and says the שטר is lost, רב יהודה believes him with a מיגו that he could have claimed he bought the field. רב זביד and רב עוירא disagree, and רבינא and רב אשי discuss how the Sura mortgage protects the owner: he pays the tax, digs the trenches, or else protests. Then רב יהודה and רב נחמן argue about an אריס who claims half while the owner says one-third. אביי explains that they truly disagree. The amud ends by asking who must bring proof when יתומים and a בעל חוב argue over who improved a field; the answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: The end of a challenge from a משנה about old trees
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes quoting a משנה: old trees a woman inherits are sold as wood, land is bought with the money, and her husband eats the produce of that land.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are sold as wood, land is bought with the money, and he eats the produce.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining in the middle of a challenge. The גמרא is finishing a quote from a משנה that treats old trees as principal that must be protected, not as produce to be used up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says the husband may not simply use up the old trees. They must be turned into land, and he only gets that land's produce. This seems to contradict a position stated just before this section, which treated old trees as something the one with rights to the produce may use up.

keyTerms.meaning: They are sold as wood (for lumber)
Produce or fruit, meaning the benefits as opposed to the principal

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a new ruling. It is the tail end of a challenge that started before this section, quoting a משנה about a married woman's inherited property.

phrases.english: they are sold as wood,
and land is bought with them,
and he eats the produce.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the husband. He gets the produce of the new land, but the land stays hers.

steps.triggerLanguage: יִמָּכְרוּ לְעֵצִים, וְיִלָּקַח בָּהֶן קַרְקַע, וְהוּא אוֹכֵל פֵּירוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a challenge begun before this section
steps.kashyaTarget: The position that old trees count as produce
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה treats old trees as principal to be preserved by buying land, not as produce the husband may use up.

steps.title: Read the משנה as 'they grew old'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers by changing the reading: the trees grew old while she owned them. They were not old when she got them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say: 'and they grew old.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by reading the משנה differently. The trees were young when she inherited them and only aged later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the trees were young and fruitful when she inherited them, the trees themselves were her principal. So even after they age, they must be protected by buying land. This is different from trees that were already old to begin with.

phrases.english: Say: and they grew old.
phrases.notes: Read it as: the trees became old later, while she owned them. They were not old when she got them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימָא: וְהִזְקִינוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 1
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the wording of the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה is about trees that were already old when inherited, so old trees are principal.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about trees that aged later. They were principal from the start, so this does not contradict the earlier position.

steps.title: Another answer: the trees were in someone else's field
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the משנה is about trees she inherited standing in a field that was not hers. The trees are all she has, so using them up would destroy the principal.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: didn't we already explain that משנה as a case where the trees came to her in a different field? There, using them up would wipe out the principal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, separate answer to the same challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If she got only the trees and not the land under them, the trees are her entire principal. If the husband used them as produce, nothing of hers would be left. That is why they must be sold and turned into land, in this case only.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces another answer)

steps.whatToRemember: Old trees can count as produce, except when they are the woman's whole principal, as in the case of trees standing in someone else's field.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
didn't we establish that one
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the משנה just quoted. The גמרא is reminding us of an explanation it already gave elsewhere.

phrases.english: as a case where they fell to her in a different field,
where the principal gets used up.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: לָאו מִי אוֹקֵימְנָא לְהַהִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, independent answer to the challenge in step 1
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה shows that old trees are always principal.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about trees without land, where the trees are the whole principal. Normally old trees can still count as produce.

steps.title: A mortgage שטר that says 'years' with no number
steps.stepSummary: A שטר gave the מלוה a field for 'years' without saying how many. The מלוה says three, the לוה says two, and the מלוה already ate the third year's fruit. Whom do we believe?
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a certain שטר that said 'years' with no number. The lender said three; the borrower said two. The lender went ahead and ate the fruit. Who is believed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: a real case about an unclear mortgage document. It ends by asking who is believed, which sets up the dispute in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Years' in plural means at least two, so both agree on two. The fight is over the third year. The מלוה has already eaten that year's fruit, so the question is whether he must pay it back.

phrases.english: There was a certain document in which was written
'years,' without a number.
The lender said: three.
The borrower said: two.
The lender went ahead and ate the produce.
phrases.notes: He ate the fruit of the third year, the year they are arguing about.

phrases.english: Who is believed?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא שְׁטָרָא דַּהֲוָה כְּתִיב בֵּיהּ שְׁנִין סְתָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new case, not connected to the old-trees discussion
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the lender or the borrower is believed about the third year, once the lender has already eaten its fruit

steps.title: רב יהודה: land stays with its owner
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says the land is presumed to belong to its owner, so the לוה is believed and the מלוה must prove his claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: land stays in the possession of its owner.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the question in favor of the borrower.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The field really belongs to the לוה, so it keeps its status as his. The מלוה, who wants the extra year, must bring proof. Without proof, he would have to return the value of the fruit he ate.

keyTerms.meaning: In the possession of its owner

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
Land stands in the possession of its owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר: קַרְקַע בְּחֶזְקַת בְּעָלֶיהָ קָיְימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The borrower is believed because land stays with its owner.

steps.title: רב כהנא: fruit stays with whoever ate it
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא disagrees. Fruit already eaten stays with the one who ate it, so the מלוה does not have to pay it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: produce stays in the possession of those who ate it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא gives the opposite answer, in favor of the lender.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב כהנא looks at the fruit, not the land. The fruit is already in the מלוה's possession, so the לוה is the one trying to take something back, and he must prove it.

keyTerms.meaning: In the possession of those who ate them

steps.confusionAlert: Both אמוראים use the idea of חזקה. They disagree about which thing to focus on: the land, which belongs to the לוה, or the fruit, which the מלוה already has.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
Produce stands in the possession of those who ate it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב כָּהֲנָא אָמַר: פֵּירוֹת בְּחֶזְקַת אוֹכְלֵיהֶן קָיְימִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב יהודה in step 5
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The lender is believed because the eaten fruit stays with him.

steps.title: The הלכה follows רב כהנא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules like רב כהנא: fruit already eaten stays with the one who ate it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is like רב כהנא, who said: produce stays in the possession of those who ate it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא decides the dispute in favor of רב כהנא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In practice, the מלוה who already ate the third year's fruit does not have to pay it back. This ruling sets up the challenge in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: And the הלכה is like him

phrases.english: And the halakha is like Rav Kahana,
who said: produce stands in the possession of those who ate it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהִלְכְתָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the dispute of steps 5 and 6
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The lender keeps the fruit he already ate.

steps.title: But we rule like רב נחמן that land stays with its owner
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ruling: we already hold the הלכה like רב נחמן, who said land stays with its owner. That sounds like רב יהודה, not רב כהנא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But don't we hold that the הלכה is like רב נחמן, who said: land stays in the possession of its owner?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a contradiction between two rulings: following רב כהנא here, and following רב נחמן elsewhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן ruled earlier in the מסכת, in a case about renting during the extra month of a leap year, that land stays with its owner. That is the same idea רב יהודה used here. So how can we rule like רב כהנא, who says the opposite?

keyTerms.meaning: But don't we hold? (introduces a challenge from an accepted ruling)

steps.whyThisMatters: The גמרא must now explain how these two rulings fit together. That explanation decides when we follow the land's owner and when we follow the one holding the fruit.

phrases.english: But don't we hold
that the halakha is like Rav Nachman,
phrases.notes: This is רב נחמן's ruling earlier in the מסכת about a rental when the year got an extra month.

phrases.english: who said: land stands in the possession of its owner!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא קַיְימָא לַן דְּהִלְכְתָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of step 7
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Ruling like רב נחמן that land stays with its owner seems to match רב יהודה and contradict ruling like רב כהנא.

steps.title: Why this case is different from רב נחמן's ruling
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן's case could never be cleared up, so the land goes back to its owner. Here the truth can still come out, so we leave the eaten fruit where it is and do not trouble the court twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the matter will never become clear. Here, the matter can become clear, and we do not make the court deal with the same case twice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 8. It explains why ruling like רב כהנא does not clash with ruling like רב נחמן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב נחמן's case the doubt can never be settled, so we fall back on the land's owner. In our case the witnesses who signed the שטר may still come forward and reveal the real number of years. If we took the fruit back from the lender now, the court might later have to reverse itself, so we leave things as they are.

keyTerms.meaning: A matter that will likely become clear later
To trouble the court with extra work

steps.whatToRemember: When the truth can still come out, we do not move money back and forth. Fruit already eaten stays with the eater, so the court does not have to rule twice.

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם – מִילְּתָא דְּלָא עֲבִידָא לְאִיגַּלּוֹיֵי הִיא.
phrases.english: There, it is a matter that will not become revealed.
phrases.notes: "There" means רב נחמן's case, where the doubt can never be cleared up.

phrases.english: Here, it is a matter that will become revealed,
phrases.notes: The witnesses who signed the שטר may still come and say what it said.

phrases.english: and troubling the court
two times, we do not trouble.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם – מִילְּתָא דְּלָא עֲבִידָא לְאִיגַּלּוֹיֵי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 8
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Following רב נחמן means the land and its fruit always go back to the owner, which would contradict רב כהנא.
steps.terutzMaskana: רב נחמן's rule applies only when the doubt can never be settled. When it can be settled, fruit already eaten stays with the eater.

steps.title: New case: five years or three, and the document is lost
steps.stepSummary: The lender says the field was given for five years and the borrower says three. The borrower asks to see the שטר, and the lender says he lost it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The lender says five years, the borrower says three. The borrower said: Bring me your document! The lender said: My document got lost.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a new case about mortgaged land. This prepares the ruling that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the dispute is five years against three. Since the lender has already held the field for three years, the question is whether he may stay for two more. Without the שטר there is no written proof, so the question is who is believed.

phrases.english: The lender says five,
the borrower says three.
He said to him: Bring me your document!
phrases.notes: The borrower is the one asking here, and he wants to see what the שטר says.

phrases.english: He said to him: The document got lost on me.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַלְוֶה אוֹמֵר חָמֵשׁ, לֹוֶה אוֹמֵר שָׁלֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new related case about mortgaged land
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the lender believed when he claims five years and says the שטר is lost?

steps.title: רב יהודה: the lender is believed because of a מיגו
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה rules that the lender is believed. He could have told a bigger lie and said he bought the field.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: The lender is believed, because if he wanted to, he could have said: The field is mine, I bought it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the case. He believes the lender.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender has held the field for three years, which is enough to support a claim that he bought it. If he were lying, he could have made that stronger claim. Since he made a smaller one, we believe him. This reasoning is called a מיגו.

keyTerms.meaning: Since he could have made a stronger claim, we believe his weaker one
"I bought it," a claim of full ownership

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: The lender is believed,
since if he wanted, he could have said:
It is purchased, in my hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the case set up in step 10
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The lender is believed because of a מיגו: he could have claimed he bought the field.
steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה: מַלְוֶה נֶאֱמָן, מִגּוֹ דְּאִי בָּעֵי אָמַר לְקוּחָה הִיא בְּיָדִי

steps.title: רב זביד and רב עוירא: the lender is really hiding the document
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא reports that רב זביד and רב עוירא disagree with רב יהודה. A lender guards his collection document, so he is probably hiding it to get two extra years.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to רב אשי: רב זביד and רב עוירא do not agree with רב יהודה. Why? A document used for collecting a debt is something a person guards carefully. He is hiding it, thinking: I will eat the field's fruit for two extra years.
steps.whatsHappening: Another opinion rejects רב יהודה's ruling. It does not trust the lender's claim that he lost the שטר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מיגו only works if we have no reason to doubt the claim. Here, "I lost it" is itself suspicious, because people keep careful watch over documents that get them their money. Since the lender is probably hiding the שטר, he is not believed.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב פָּפָּא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Rav Ashi:
Rav Zevid and Rav Avira

phrases.aramaic: לָא סְבִירָא לְהוּ הָא דְּרַב יְהוּדָה.
phrases.english: do not hold of this ruling of Rav Yehuda.
What is the reason?
This document, since it stands ready for collecting,
he is surely careful with it,
and it is hiding that he hid his document,
he thinks: I will eat it for two extra years.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב זְבִיד וְרַב עַוִּירָא לָא סְבִירָא לְהוּ הָא דְּרַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב יהודה's ruling in step 11
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole ruling of רב יהודה that the lender is believed
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The claim "I lost the שטר" is not believable, because people guard their collection documents. The lender is likely hiding it, so his מיגו does not help.

steps.title: רבינא: would the Sura mortgage let lenders steal land?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא challenges רב יהודה's ruling. In Sura the mortgage document says the land goes back to the owner after the set years. If a lender could hide that document and claim he bought the land, the Sages would have created a system that causes loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: If so, think of the Sura mortgage, where they write: "When these years are over, this land goes back without money." If the lender hid the mortgage document and said "I bought it," would he be believed? Would the Sages set up something that leads to a loss?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא attacks רב יהודה's מיגו. He shows that it would lead to an unacceptable result in the Sura mortgage system.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רב יהודה, a lender who has held land for three years can claim he bought it. In a Sura mortgage, though, the lender always holds the land for years, so any lender could hide the document and claim ownership. The Sages would never set up an arrangement that lets owners lose their land this way.

keyTerms.meaning: "If that is so," used to introduce a challenge that pushes a view to its result
The Sura mortgage, where the land returns to the owner after a set number of years with no payment

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:
But if so,
this mortgage of Sura, where they write like this:
"When these years are completed,
this land shall go out without money."
Where he hid the mortgage document
and said: It is purchased, in my hand,
would he also be believed?
Would the Sages set up a matter
that leads to a loss?
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, הַאי מַשְׁכַּנְתָּא דְסוּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to רב יהודה's מיגו and challenges it from a practical case
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's ruling in step 11 that the lender is believed with a מיגו of "I bought it"
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If holding land for years lets a lender claim ownership, every Sura mortgage holder could steal the land. The Sages would not have set up a system that causes such loss.

steps.title: רב אשי: in Sura the owner pays the taxes and digs the trenches
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that in a Sura mortgage, the Sages arranged for the owner to keep paying the land tax and digging the trenches. Everyone can see it is still his land, so the lender cannot claim he bought it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There, the Sages arranged that the landowner pays the land tax and digs the irrigation trenches.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי defends רב יהודה's ruling. He shows that the Sura case is different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the owner keeps paying the tax and doing the upkeep, his ownership stays public. A lender's claim "I bought it" would not be believed there, so he has no מיגו. In an ordinary mortgage there is no such public sign, so רב יהודה's מיגו still holds.

keyTerms.meaning: Digs the trenches, for watering the field

steps.whatToRemember: A מיגו of "I bought it" works only when nothing shows the land still belongs to the owner. In Sura, paying the tax and digging the trenches show clearly whose land it is.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב אשי answering רבינא.

phrases.english: There, the Sages arranged for him
that the owner of the land pays the land tax
and digs the trenches.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם תַּקִּינוּ לֵיה רַבָּנַן דְּמָרֵי אַרְעָא יָהֵיב טַסְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's קשיא in step 13
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב יהודה's מיגו would let any Sura mortgage holder claim to own the land.
steps.terutzMaskana: In Sura the owner pays the tax and digs the trenches, so his ownership is publicly known and the lender has no believable claim of purchase.

steps.title: What about land with no trenches and no tax?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא challenges רב אשי's answer by asking about land where there is no trench work and no tax, so nothing public shows who owns it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Land that needs no trenches and pays no tax: what then?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא pushes back on רב אשי's answer from Step 14. He asks what protects the owner when his land has no trenches and no tax.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי said everyone can see the owner still owns the land because he digs the trenches and pays the tax. Some land has neither, so that public sign is missing. In that case the lender could hide the document and claim he bought the field, and the original problem comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: Trenches or ditches dug around a field, the owner's job
The land tax paid to the king

phrases.english: Land that has no need for trenches
and he does not pay tax on it, what then?
phrases.notes: "He" is the owner. With no trenches and no tax, nothing public shows the land is still his.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַרְעָא דְּלֵית לַהּ כַּרְיָא וְלָא יָהֵיב טַסְקָא, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the limits of רב אשי's answer in Step 14
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's answer that trench work and tax payment show public ownership
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Where no trench work or tax exists, the public sign is missing, so the Sages' system could still cause a loss.

steps.title: The owner should have protested
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that in such a case the owner should have made a public protest.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: He should have protested.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers רבינא. When there is no public sign of ownership, the owner has to protest out loud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the land itself shows nothing, the owner must make his ownership known himself. He should announce that the land is his before the lender holds it long enough to claim it. The protection now comes from the owner's own action, not from a built-in arrangement of the Sages.

keyTerms.meaning: He should have, he needed to

phrases.english: He said to him: He should have protested!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִיבְּעִי לֵיהּ לְמַחוֹיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 15
steps.terutzResolutionType: Places the responsibility on the owner to protect himself
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without trenches or tax, the owner has no protection and the Sages' system causes loss
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner can protect himself by protesting, so the system does not cause loss

steps.title: What if he did not protest?
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks what the law is if the owner did not protest.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he did not protest, what then?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא asks a follow-up question. What happens if the owner never protested?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי said the owner should protest. Now רבינא asks about an owner who failed to do it. Does the lender win?

phrases.english: If he did not protest, what then?
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some don't. The word in square brackets is the corrected reading: "protested."

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא (אִימְּחָא) [מַחִי], מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follow-up question on רב אשי's answer in Step 16
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The ruling when the owner failed to protest

steps.title: He caused his own loss
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that an owner who did not protest caused his own loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: He is the one who caused his own loss.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers that if the owner did not protest, the loss is his own fault.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Sages are not to blame, because the owner had a way to protect himself and did not use it. So the Sura mortgage system does not cause loss. A loss only comes from the owner's own carelessness.

keyTerms.meaning: He caused a loss to himself

steps.whatToRemember: In a Sura mortgage, the owner is protected by paying the tax and digging the trenches. Where those don't apply, he must protest. If he doesn't, the loss is his own fault.

phrases.english: He is the one who caused a loss to himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיהוּ הוּא דְּאַפְסֵיד אַנַּפְשֵׁיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 17
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The owner who did not protest bears his own loss, so the Sages' system is not to blame

steps.title: Sharecropper says half, owner says one-third
steps.stepSummary: A new case: the sharecropper claims he was promised half the crop, and the owner says one-third. Who is believed?
steps.simpleTranslation: A sharecropper says: I came on for half. The owner says: I brought him on for one-third. Who is believed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a brand-new case and asks a question. It sets up the dispute that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אריס works someone else's field in return for a share of the crop. Here the two sides disagree about how big that share was supposed to be. Neither side has proof, so the question is whose word we accept.

keyTerms.meaning: A sharecropper who works a field for a share of the crop

phrases.english: A sharecropper says: I came down to the field for half,
phrases.notes: "Came down" is the usual way of saying he started working the field.

phrases.english: and the owner says: I brought him down for one-third,
who is believed?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָרִיס אוֹמֵר: לְמֶחֱצָה יָרַדְתִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the Sura mortgage
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whose claim is accepted when a sharecropper and owner disagree about the share

steps.title: רב יהודה and רב נחמן disagree
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says the owner is believed. רב נחמן says everything follows local custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: The owner is believed. רב נחמן said: Everything follows the local custom.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים give different answers to the question. One believes the owner, and the other goes by what is normal in that place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה accepts the owner's word. רב נחמן does not look at either person's claim. He assumes they made the usual deal for that area, so the sharecropper gets whatever sharecroppers normally get there.

keyTerms.meaning: The local custom of the region

phrases.aramaic: רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר: בַּעַל הַבַּיִת נֶאֱמָן.
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: The owner is believed.

phrases.aramaic: רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר: הַכֹּל כְּמִנְהַג הַמְּדִינָה.
phrases.english: Rav Nachman said: Everything follows the local custom.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר: בַּעַל הַבַּיִת נֶאֱמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives two answers to the question in Step 19
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב יהודה: the owner is believed. רב נחמן: follow the local custom.

steps.title: At first they thought there was no real argument
steps.stepSummary: People first understood that רב יהודה and רב נחמן do not argue. Each one is talking about a different kind of place.
steps.simpleTranslation: They understood from this that they do not argue: one is speaking about a place where sharecroppers take half, and the other about a place where sharecroppers take one-third.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings an early way of understanding the two opinions so that they don't clash. This sets up the next step, which rejects it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a place where sharecroppers usually get half, the sharecropper is believed. That is רב נחמן's case. In a place where they usually get one-third, the owner is believed, which matches רב יהודה. So both rulings really just follow the custom.

keyTerms.meaning: They understood from it, they assumed

steps.confusionAlert: This is only an early assumption, not the final answer. The very next step rejects it.

phrases.english: They understood from it that they do not disagree:
this one is in a place where the sharecropper takes half,
phrases.notes: This is רב נחמן's case, where custom backs the sharecropper's claim of half.

phrases.english: that one is in a place where the sharecropper takes one-third.
phrases.notes: This is רב יהודה's case, where custom backs the owner.

steps.triggerLanguage: סְבוּר מִינַּהּ לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to reconcile the two opinions in Step 20
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Early assumption: both rulings follow local custom, each in a different kind of place

steps.title: אביי: they disagree even where half is the custom
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי quotes אביי. They disagree even where sharecroppers take half, and רב יהודה believes the owner because he could have said the worker was only a hired hand or a gleaner.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי, son of שמואל's daughter, told them: This is what אביי said. They argue even in a place where sharecroppers take half. רב יהודה said the owner is believed, because if he wanted he could have said: He is my hired worker or my gleaner.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרי rejects the idea that the two don't argue. Quoting אביי, he shows they really do argue, and he gives רב יהודה's reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even where custom says half, רב יהודה still believes the owner. The owner could have told a bigger lie and said the man was never a sharecropper at all, only a paid worker or a gleaner with no share in the crop. Since he only claims one-third, we believe him, the same "he could have told a bigger lie" reasoning רב יהודה used in Step 11.

keyTerms.meaning: My hired worker, paid a set wage
My gleaner, an occasional worker with no set share

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows רב יהודה follows one steady approach: a person who could have made a stronger false claim is believed when he makes a weaker one.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב מָרִי בְּרַהּ דְּבַת שְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: Rav Mari, the son of Shmuel's daughter, said to them:
This is what Abaye said:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ בְּאַתְרָא דְּשָׁקֵיל אֲרִיסָא פַּלְגָא פְּלִיגִי,
phrases.english: Even in a place where the sharecropper takes half, they disagree,

phrases.aramaic: רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר: בַּעַל הַבַּיִת נֶאֱמָן,
phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: The owner is believed,
because if he wanted, he could have said:
He is my hired worker or my gleaner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב מָרִי בְּרַהּ דְּבַת שְׁמוּאֵל: הָכִי אָמַר אַבָּיֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reconciliation in Step 21
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the claim that רב יהודה and רב נחמן do not argue
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב יהודה believes the owner even where custom is half, because the owner could have claimed the worker had no share at all

steps.title: Orphans and creditor argue over who improved the field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the orphans say they improved the field and the creditor says their father did, which side must bring proof?
steps.simpleTranslation: If the orphans say 'We improved the field,' and the creditor says 'Your father improved it,' who has to bring proof?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a brand-new question about a fight between יתומים and a בעל חוב over who added value to the field. It only asks the question here; the answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Who made the improvement decides who gets its value. If the father improved the field, the improvement was part of what was owed to the creditor, so he collects it. If the orphans improved it after his death, that added value is theirs, and the creditor cannot simply take it. The question is who must prove their side of the story.

keyTerms.meaning: Orphans: here, the children who inherited the borrower's field
We improved it. The field became worth more because of our work
Creditor: the lender who is owed money
Upon whom is it to bring proof? This asks who carries the burden of proof

steps.confusionAlert: This is a new case, not more of the sharecropper case from the steps before. Only the general theme carries over: two sides disagree, and we must decide whose word holds.

phrases.english: The orphans say: We improved [the field],
and the creditor says: Your father improved it,
upon whom is it to bring proof?

steps.triggerLanguage: עַל מִי לְהָבִיא רְאָיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case, similar in style to the sharecropper dispute. Again two sides disagree and the גמרא must decide whose claim is accepted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which side, the orphans or the creditor, carries the burden of proving who improved the field?
